title: Donations & the Ending
content_html:
The Donation Cycle

The final phase of the clones’ lives is the donation cycle. Clones make up to four donations before they “complete” — the euphemism for dying on the operating table. Before donating, some clones serve as “carers” — looking after other clones through their donation process. Kathy has been a carer for almost twelve years when the novel opens, an unusually long tenure that gives her time to reflect on her life.

Key Fact

Ishiguro’s euphemisms are central to the novel’s horror. ‘Donations’ disguises organ harvesting. ‘Completions’ disguises death. ‘Carers’ disguises accomplices. These words allow society — and the clones themselves — to avoid confronting the brutality of the system. Language becomes a tool of control, making the unspeakable speakable and the unacceptable routine.

Ruth donates and completes before Kathy and Tommy. On her deathbed, she makes a devastating confession: she deliberately kept Kathy and Tommy apart because she was jealous of their connection. She urges them to find Madame and apply for a deferral, giving them her belief that love can buy them time.

Tommy’s Last Hope

After Ruth’s death, Kathy and Tommy finally become a couple. Tommy works feverishly on his tiny animal drawings, convinced they will prove to Madame that he and Kathy have souls — that their love is real and deserves time. The intensity of his hope is both beautiful and unbearable. Ishiguro makes the reader hope alongside Tommy, knowing this hope will be crushed.

Kathy and Tommy travel to visit Madame and Miss Emily. They present Tommy’s art and ask for a deferral. The scene is one of the most painful in modern literature. Miss Emily tells them the truth: deferrals never existed. The Gallery was used to prove clones have souls, as part of a campaign for humane treatment — a campaign that ultimately failed. “We didn’t have the Gallery to look into your souls. We had the Gallery to see if you had souls at all.” Tommy and Kathy leave with nothing. Their love cannot save them.

Tommy’s Scream

After leaving Madame’s house, Tommy asks Kathy to stop the car. He gets out and screams into the darkness — a raw, animal howl of grief and rage. This is the only moment in the novel where a character openly rebels against their fate. Kathy holds him. The scene is devastating because it is so brief: Tommy’s scream is the only crack in the novel’s emotional restraint, and it is immediately followed by a return to quiet acceptance.

Key Fact

Tommy’s scream is the novel’s only moment of open rebellion. It breaks through the restraint that characterises the entire narrative. The scream expresses everything the clones have been conditioned not to feel: rage, injustice, refusal. But it is immediately contained — Kathy holds him, they return to the car, and the system continues. Ishiguro shows that even rebellion is absorbed by the structures of compliance.

The Final Pages

Tommy completes after his fourth donation. Kathy narrates his death with characteristic restraint: “He looked peaceful enough.” The understatement is gutting. In the novel’s final paragraphs, Kathy stands alone in a Norfolk field, imagining that all the things she has lost — Tommy, Ruth, Hailsham, her childhood — might wash up on the shore. She knows this is fantasy, but she allows herself the moment before driving away to begin her own donations.

The image of Kathy in the Norfolk field is the novel’s most powerful moment. The field is empty. The shore yields nothing. Lost things do not come back. Yet Kathy’s willingness to stand there and imagine — to hold onto feeling despite knowing it changes nothing — is profoundly human. Ishiguro’s final message is paradoxical: the clones are most fully human in the moments when they confront their own mortality, just as all humans are defined by their awareness of death.

Kathy’s closing words — “I just waited a bit, then turned back to the car, to drive off to wherever it was I was supposed to be” — encapsulate the novel’s themes. “Wherever I was supposed to be” accepts the system while acknowledging its cruelty. The passive construction (“supposed to be”) reflects a life lived according to others’ decisions. Yet the act of narrating — of telling her story — is itself a form of resistance, asserting that her life mattered.

Key Fact

“I just waited a bit, then turned back to the car, to drive off to wherever it was I was supposed to be.” The passive ‘supposed to be’ shows a life controlled by others. The restraint mirrors Kathy’s character throughout. Yet the act of telling her story asserts that her life mattered — narration as the only form of resistance available to her.
exam_tip_html: The ending is the strongest material for part (b) responses. Analyse the specific language: “supposed to be” (passive, controlled), “waited a bit” (restraint, resignation), the Norfolk field (empty hope). Link to AO3: Ishiguro’s theme of mortality. A top-band response would argue that the novel’s devastation comes from restraint, not melodrama — and that Kathy’s narration is itself a form of quiet resistance.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ishiguro’s euphemisms (‘donations,’ ‘completions,’ ‘carers’) are tools of linguistic control that make the horrifying routine.
  • Tommy’s scream is the novel’s only moment of open rebellion, immediately contained by the structures of compliance.
  • Kathy’s final image in the Norfolk field is paradoxically hopeful: standing in emptiness, she asserts her humanity through the act of remembering and narrating.

glossary_terms.definition: The process by which clones give organs in a series of operations until they die.
The euphemism for a clone’s death after their final organ donation.
A style characterised by understatement and suppressed emotion.
A clone who looks after other clones during their donation process, before beginning their own.
A grammatical structure where the subject receives the action, suggesting lack of agency.
